Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
The people responsible have faced no consequences
There is something wrong with me as a person

vignette: Sergeant Malik's memories flood back whenever he hears the whistle of a police officer at the base's perimeter, sees a familiar face in the mess hall, or smells sweat in the field. Each trigger forces him to refuse the uniform he once wore with pride, skip the scheduled PT, and steer clear of the civilian crowd he had served with his medical kit. Even the briefest glimpse of a police badge or a family photograph in the mess hall awakens Malik's fragmented recollections of the night his girlfriend assaulted him in a cramped apartment, the way her hands tightened around his jaw, and the lingering sting of a broken arm. The constant reminder of authority figures and the smell of sweat erodes Malik's sense of purpose, making him believe that life has lost its meaning, that those who harmed him have escaped unpunished, and that something fundamentally wrong lies within him. Feeling defective and powerless, Malik deliberately avoids any clothing that resembles the red bandage on his former arm, refuses to participate in the squad's drills, and withdraws from conversations with coworkers, believing that contact will only expose his fragile state. His conviction that the world no longer honors justice magnifies the sense of danger he feels whenever an officer's footsteps echo, a familiar laugh surfaces, or a familiar scent rises, forcing him into a perpetual state of alertness. The belief that he is defective fuels the intensity of his flashbacks; each time he feels a slight threat, the memory of the night's violence sharpens, replaying the bruise marks and the raw pain as if it were happening again. During a vivid recollection of his body being twisted, Malik instinctively withdraws from the mess hall, avoids the gym, and refuses any uniform that reminds him of the night, convinced these actions will keep the memories from surfacing. When the painful recollection surfaces, Malik's heart races and his ears ring with the imagined gunshots of that night, reinforcing his belief that danger lurks even in the quiet of his own sleeping quarters. The vividness of the memory makes Malik feel that his life has been irrevocably shattered, that no one can hold him accountable, and that he is a broken person forever marked by that night, yet he cannot articulate the scene in words. After each alarm that sounds like a police siren, Malik's heightened vigilance pushes him to skip PT, wear loose clothing that does not echo his bandaged arm, and isolate himself from any gathering that might trigger a memory. The constant state of alertness turns even the faint rustle of leaves into a potential echo of gunfire, and Malik finds himself reliving the assault whenever a subtle sound rises in his sleeping quarters. Each perceived danger reinforces Malik's conviction that he is forever vulnerable, that justice will never come, and that he has become a defective survivor trapped in a cycle of fear. The ever-present threat of police footsteps, familiar voices, or the smell of sweat makes Malik hyper-vigilant, turning ordinary sights, sounds, and scents into immediate alarms that trigger his avoidance patterns. By refusing to face his routine duties, Malik keeps his memories raw and vivid; the avoidance acts as a conduit that constantly re-activates the night's trauma whenever he finally confronts a similar situation. Each time he withdraws, Malik's belief that he is unworthy of trust and that his past defines his entire identity is strengthened, deepening his sense of defectiveness. His avoidance of familiar clothing and people heightens his awareness of any resemblance or presence, causing even a stray uniform patch or a friendly smile to become potential triggers that flood his mind with dread. By not engaging in physical training or social interactions, Malik's baseline level of alertness climbs, making him feel perpetually exposed and further inflating his perception of threat. Now, at nearly fifty, Malik has stopped answering radio calls, begun to lose sleep, and feels isolated in the barracks. He finally sought help because the relentless cycle of triggers, memories, and fear had begun to fracture his sense of duty, leaving him terrified that his own life might once again be claimed by an unseen threat.
